name: drop_in_place
declaration: unsafe fn drop_in_place < T : ? Sized > (to_drop : * mut T)
rules: `to_drop` must be valid for both reads and writes of the pointed-to `T`. For nonzero-sized accesses, this requires, but is not necessarily ensured by, the entire accessed memory range being within the bounds of the allocated object determined by the pointer's provenance.
`to_drop` must be properly aligned for `T`, even if `T` has size 0.
`to_drop` must be nonnull, even if `T` has size 0.
The value pointed to by `to_drop` must be valid for dropping, including any additional invariants required by its type; for example, a `Box`'s pointer to the heap must be valid.

While `drop_in_place` is executing, parts of the value pointed to by `to_drop` may be accessed only through the `&mut self` references supplied to the `Drop::drop` methods that `drop_in_place` invokes.
Memory accesses performed by `drop_in_place` are non-atomic; concurrent accesses to the same location from different threads cause undefined behavior unless both accesses only read memory.

If `to_drop` is obtained by casting a reference to a pointer, its validity for memory access is guaranteed while the underlying object is live and no reference is used to access the same memory; reference and raw-pointer accesses cannot be interleaved under this guarantee.
If `T` is not `Copy`, using the pointed-to value after calling `drop_in_place` can cause undefined behavior; assigning with `*to_drop = foo` counts as such a use because it drops the value again.
`drop_in_place` may be used to drop pinned data when `T` is not `repr(packed)`, provided the pinned data has not been moved before it is dropped.
